about.title: Napa Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A product does not have to be exotic to cause serious harm. In a city of about 80,000 people, the everyday items are the ones that matter most: a space heater in a Browns Valley home, a pressure washer at a tasting room off Rt 29, a space-saving e-bike ridden down Soscol Avenue, or a child's car seat on the way to school. When one of those fails because of how it was designed, how it was built, or how it was labeled, Napa County residents may have a claim under California product liability law. What sets these cases apart is strict liability. You generally do not have to prove the company was careless, only that the product was defective and that the defect caused your injury. Manufacturers, distributors, and the local retailer who sold it can all share responsibility. Keep the product, the packaging, and any receipts. LawProactive will connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney who handles these claims on contingency.

items.question: I was hurt by a piece of winery or cellar equipment while working near Napa. Is that a product liability claim or a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: It can be both. Workers' compensation typically covers on-the-job injuries regardless of fault, but if a pump, press, forklift, or other piece of equipment was defective, a separate product liability claim may exist against the company that made or sold it. An attorney can sort out how the two interact so nothing is left on the table.

items.question: Do I have to prove the manufacturer was negligent?
items.answer: Usually not. California product liability often operates under strict liability, meaning you generally need to show the product had a design, manufacturing, or warning defect and that the defect caused your injury. Whether the company acted carelessly is typically not the central question.

items.question: What should I do with the product that injured me?
items.answer: Keep it exactly as it is, along with the box, manual, and proof of purchase if you have them. Do not repair it, return it to the store, or throw it away, because the physical item is often the most important evidence in the case. Photograph it and the scene, then reach out so an attorney can advise on secure storage.
